By Reshmi BasuNovember 2, 2026 at 9:56 PM UTCBookmark

Insurance brokerage and fintech Acrisure reported third-quarter earnings that showed an improvement in broker retention, after a period in which it inadvertently gave creditors access to an internal spreadsheet then demanded they not act on the financial metrics they might have seen.
The company told investors Monday that retail broker retention in North America for the period was 84.2%, up from 82.3% in the second quarter of this year, according to people familiar with the matter. The improved retention figures helped offset a $131 million cash burn during the period, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private information.

For almost three months, Big Tech companies didn’t borrow in the US bond market after they spooked investors with a debt binge in the hundreds of billions of dollars. Now they’re flooding in again.
Oracle Corp. was selling $10 billion of bonds on Monday alongside an equal amount of equity, while Meta Platforms Inc. is eyeingBloomberg Terminal
at least $20 billion from a potential sale in multiple currencies. On Thursday, Microsoft Corp. sold $25 billion of bonds, its first US offering since 2017. The deluge is coming in other currencies too. Alphabet Inc. sold debt in the Europe bond market on Monday for the second time this year.

Most emerging-market currencies advanced Monday after Iran’s supreme leader authorized the government to hold peace talks, easing concerns over the conflict in the Middle East and stoking a slump in oil prices.
Currencies from Chile, Hungary and South Africa were among the biggest gainers as Brent crude tumbled about 11% to trade near $104 per barrel. The Mexican peso rallied the most since April, while Asian currencies slipped. The index for developing-world equities rose.

The Securities and Exchange Commission should add the European Union to a four-decade old list of exempted issuers, a move that would ease restrictions on US investor access to the bloc’s new bond futures market, according to a group representing hedge funds.
The US-based Managed Funds Association, which represents the global alternative asset management industry, said in a letter to the SEC that it supports a proposal to exempt the EU from rules governing security futures. Such contracts are jointly regulated by the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, while futures on certain exempted government bonds fall exclusively under CFTC jurisdiction.

As gold heads toward its worst annual loss in more than a decade, investors are gauging the odds a political shift in the US will restore the precious metal’s haven allure.
Usually, bullion is a safe place to hide during periods of persistent global friction, but after starting the year with a momentum-fueled ride to a record of over $5,500 an ounce, gold now trades below $4,000. The artificial intelligence investment boom, soaring bond yields and interest rate-hike expectations have pummeled the yellow metal, sending it down more than 8% so far in 2026.

Technology stocks led US equities lower on Monday as worries around the artificial intelligence trade outweighed hopes of US-Iran diplomacy.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index ended down 1.4%, pushing it into a correction, when shares lose 10% from their last peak in October. The S&P 500 Index fell by 0.5%. Both gauges failed to maintain gains from earlier in the session. Energy and information technology led declines as crude prices fell after reports that US President Donald Trump signaled progress toward peace talks with Iran.
